newsitem.title: UK: Emerging market gains seen continuing.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market gains seen continuing.

text.p: Another strong showing from emerging markets last week defied predictions that a correction was due, and analysts said a strong upward trend remains intact.
They said political factors threatened short term gains in some countries, but a recent broad-based rally should continue for much of 1997.

"Emerging markets have been underperforming for well over three years, I think it is about time they started outperforming significantly. I think this is the year of outperformance for emerging markets," said Pictet senior investment manager Douglas Polunin.

In ROMANIA, the government should announce a tough reform package on Monday. A statement said Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea would announce reforms of the economy, coupled with social protection steps.

The IMF and World Bank have been working with the government for over a month on the reforms, including faster restructuring and privatisation of industries, as well as price and currency markets liberalisation.
Bucharest is seeking up to $1.0 billion in total loans from the IMF and the World Bank needed to push through with its reform drive.

Ciorbea on Friday called for support for planned tough reforms, saying they were crucial if his country wanted to avoid a crisis similar to that in Bulgaria. He also said his government planned to speed the selloff of state banks.
Polunin said a further correction was possible in TURKEY, but the market was set for longer term gains.
Turkish stocks were easier on Friday amid concern that Moody's may downgrade it Ba3 Turkey rating and on political concerns. Moody's put Turkey on credit watch last month.
Polunin is positive on PAKISTAN, INDONESIA and GREECE, and expects emerging Europe to lead gains in emerging markets in 1997.
BULGARIA's caretaker cabinet spends its first week in office after parliament was dissolved on February 19.
A delegation from the European Union is expected this week, and the government is also expected to entertain the IMF soon.

Finance minister Svetoslav Gavriisky said the country would rely on external loans to repay foreign debt of some $1 billion due this year. He hopes to receive between $300 million to $400 million from the EU.
SLOVENIA's prime minister-designate Janez Drnovsek continues his coalition talks with rightist parties which hold 44 out of 90 parliamentary seats.
But analysts warn that a new election is increasingly likely.

"Should Drnovsek attempts to gain additional support fail, President Kucan will have to nominate a new prime minister, probably M Podobnik, the leader of the opposition centre-right Slovene Spring Alliance. A new election is increasingly likely," CSFB said in a research report.
In RUSSIA, the watch on President Boris Yeltsin's health continues. The Duma lower house rejected a resolution on Friday calling for Yeltsin to quit on health grounds. The move had no legal force.
In ECUADOR, gains are expected following the installation of Fabian Alarcon as president, ANZ said in a weekly comment.

"After the incompetence of (Abdala) Bucaram, Ecuador can now look forward to a period of stability, with coherent and structured economic reform and the new administration pledging to tackle the fiscal deficit," it said.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, denominated in dollars, was up 1.9 percent week-on-week by Monday morning at 328.50 points. It is up 11.4 percent so far in 1997.
Latin America was up 3.6 percent at 625.98, Asia was up 0.9 percent at 265.20, and Europe, Middle East and Africa was quoted at 158.34, up 1.5 percent.
Asian emerging markets continue to lag other emerging market gains, although INDONESIA is attracting interest as investors focus on a healthy economic situation and corporate earnings.

In SOUTH AFRICA, funds continue to renew their interest following a volatile 1996. Gilt buyers have driven foreign inflows, and Santander Investment says Finance Minister Trevor Manuel will have to tread carefully in his March budget "if this new dawn is not to fade".
